title: Do we REALLY want Teachers to be more like Doctors?
author: Science of Reading Classroom
summary: The author pushes back on the popular demand that teachers be more like doctors and simply follow the research. She argues that doctors resist new evidence just as teachers do, citing a dermatologist example and the slow adoption of antibiotics for ulcers, because people are biased toward stasis. She then questions the massive state investment in LETRS-style knowledge-first training, drawing on Thomas Guskey's critique that this theory of change rests on 1930s research. Guskey's alternative holds that beliefs change only after teachers try a practice and see it work for their students. The post turns this into a design for professional development that is practical, modeled, rehearsed, followed up and patient. The classification is Practice & Culture because the argument concerns how teachers change and how PD and school leaders should support them, not what to teach.
points: Resistance to evidence is a human trait, not a teacher defect, so the doctor comparison used to scold teachers is both unfair and inaccurate.
Knowledge-first PD such as LETRS is a costly bet on a theory of change that Guskey says has little evidence behind it, especially for veteran teachers.
Guskey's model reverses the order: practice and visible student success come first, and belief follows.
Effective PD gets teachers implementing quickly with video models, rehearsal and prepared materials rather than more theory.
Leaders must supply regular follow-up, collective accountability and patience, and prioritize a few changes rather than everything at once.
quotes: In other words, teachers are like doctors–and doctors are like teachers. They’re just human beings, who are heavily biased towards stasis. And it’s hard to change people’s beliefs and attitudes, especially when they’ve been prescribing the same medication or teaching reading the same way for the last 20 plus years.

But according to Thomas Guskey, this theory of professional development rests on old and outdated research from the 1930s. There is little indication that this sort of knowledge-first professional development impacts teacher practice, especially among veteran teachers.

Guskey’s model argues that teacher beliefs and attitudes change only after they change their practice and see the impact on student learning. In Guskey’s telling, “the crucial point is that it is not the professional development per se, but the experience of successful implementation that changes teachers’ attitudes and beliefs. They believe it works because they have seen it work, and that experience shapes their attitudes and beliefs.” In other words? Doing and seeing enable believing.

Professional development should be more practical and less theoretical. It should be designed to get teachers implementing and experimenting with the desired practice or materials as quickly as possible. To achieve this, it also needs to include models (videos!) of other teachers teaching, opportunities for teacher rehearsal, prepared materials–whatever it takes to get teachers doing the work.

Even with all of the best supports in place, changing instructional practice is hard work. As teachers implement, they need planned opportunities where they discuss, refine, and compare their work and experiences. These follow-ups help build culture around instructional improvement by reinforcing the shared commitment to the hard work of improving instruction.

This approach to professional development will only work if teachers have the time to experiment, refine, and be honest about what’s going well and what’s not going well. Moreover, we can’t reasonably expect teachers to change everything at once. That’s a recipe for cognitive overload and failure, so leaders need to prioritize.
